responses.strategic_rationale: The Bonn residential parasomnia unit must reconcile rigorous data quality with feasible throughput, while maintaining participant safety, privacy, and funding stability. The levers target critical decision points: pacing of capacity expansion, modality mix and sensing rigor, recruitment effectiveness, data governance, funding architecture, and automated event triage. By embedding gates, staged deployments, and metric-driven sequencing, the plan can validate the residential capture model, enable longitudinal phenotyping, and produce robust methods-validation outputs without prematurely committing to a fully scalable diagnostic platform.

levers.name: Deferral of additional suites until pilot data quality thresholds are demonstrated
levers.consequences: Delaying expansion preserves data integrity and safety during the pilot and avoids oversaturation, but it slows enrollment momentum. The gap is the absence of explicit, measurable ramp thresholds that account for night-to-night variability and site performance when deciding the next capacity step.
options: Proceed with 12-suite expansion only after the pilot demonstrates high data quality, acceptable false-alarm rates, and verified annotation throughput across a representative sample of nights.
Maintain an 8-suite launch and optimize scheduling, staffing, and night coverage to maximize usable data without expanding capacity.
Test a modular annex to add two temporary suites under flexible lease terms while collecting performance metrics and user feedback to inform a future expansion decision.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off: delaying expansion preserves quality but slows throughput; the gap is the absence of explicit ramp thresholds and a plan that accommodates night-to-night variability.

levers.name: Sensing architecture optimization path
levers.consequences: Shifting modalities changes signal quality, data storage, and staffing needs; enhancing data richness can improve event characterization but raises maintenance overhead. The gap is a clear, quantitative mapping from modality changes to expected improvements in detection sensitivity and annotation throughput.
options: Calibrate and stabilize baseline dry-electrode EEG, mattress sensors, and infrared cameras to establish a robust, low-burden data baseline before adding higher-cost modalities.
Introduce richer PSG components only on enhanced nights after automated quality checks demonstrate consistent data capture from baseline modalities.
Phase in privacy-preserving data streams by adding environmental sensors with strict access controls and on-demand de-identified exports.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off: richer sensing improves data but increases cost and burden; the gap is missing explicit thresholds tying modality expansion to measurable gains.

levers.name: Tiered recruitment funnel with structured pre-screening
levers.consequences: Balancing inclusivity with data consistency reduces screen-failures but may slow participant intake and prolong the study timeline. The gap is lack of a real-time monitoring dashboard to adjust inclusion criteria and incentives based on observed yield.
options: Implement a tiered pre-screening funnel with structured clinical interviews and collateral history to minimize screen-failures and align enrollment with event-yield targets.
Offer transportation stipends and flexible scheduling to boost participation while maintaining inclusion criteria that support consistent data collection.
Engage matched controls via hospital networks to streamline comparisons without broadening the enrollment base.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off: stricter screening improves data consistency but slows enrollment; the gap is lacking a live yield-tracking mechanism to tune criteria responsively.

levers.name: Privacy-preserving data-sharing governance with staged data releases
levers.consequences: Expanding data sharing increases visibility and collaboration but heightens privacy risk; the gap is lacking concrete governance details to enforce consent, de-identification, and access controls during multi-party use.
options: Publish de-identified physiological and sensor datasets under strict data-use agreements to balance openness with participant privacy.
Implement opt-in video masking for bedroom footage with strict governance to preserve privacy while enabling supplementary behavioral analyses.
Phase data releases with controlled access portals, granting subsets to trusted collaborators before wider dissemination.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off: openness vs. privacy; the gap is a concrete governance framework detailing consent processes, de-identification standards, and access controls.

levers.name: Industry partnership terms that protect publication rights
levers.consequences: Industry funding can accelerate progress but may influence dissemination; the gap is ensuring terms and a governance mechanism that prevents delayed publications or biased reporting while preserving academic autonomy.
options: Negotiate industry collaborations with explicit publication rights and data access terms that preserve core academic outputs.
Pursue additional non-dilutive public funding and European research consortia to extend the pilot and widen data resources.
Form a multi-site grant proposal with other sleep centers to share recruitment and cross-site validation while maintaining independent publication rights.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off: industry involvement risks publication control; the gap is lacking clear, enforceable terms that safeguard timely, unbiased reporting.

levers.name: Semi-automated event triage with human-in-the-loop
levers.consequences: Automation reduces manual review load but can miss subtle events or introduce biases if not properly calibrated. The gap is a robust fallback for disagreements between algorithm flags and human scorers.
options: Prototype a semi-automated event triage pipeline that flags high-fidelity events for rapid double-scored review by two independent raters.
Strengthen scorer reliability by instituting blinded scoring rounds and standardized calibration sessions before official scoring.
Schedule regular retrospective audits of algorithm-flagged events to identify biases and adjust weighting thresholds accordingly.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off: automation vs. detection gaps; the gap is a defined mechanism for resolving disagreements and correcting biases over time.

responses.strategic_rationale: The Bonn residential sleep unit operates at the intersection of restricted physical capacity and a data-rich, multi-stream sensing pipeline. Core tensions include delivering high-quality parasomnia data within safety and privacy constraints while achieving timely recruitment, sustainable staffing, and rigorous validation of semi-automated event-triage tools. The levers below challenge assumptions about where flexibility yields the most value: expanding recruitment and cross-site collaboration, optimizing sensing and governance, strengthening safety and staffing, and designing funding and publication structures that preserve scientific credibility. Prioritization should balance speed, data quality, and ethical risk as the facility scales.

levers.name: Regional collaboration for participant funnel optimization
levers.consequences: Expands enrollment velocity and diversifies the participant pool, accelerating progress toward Aim 1. However, it introduces cross-site governance and potential variability in screening quality unless SOPs and IRB approvals are harmonized.
options: Formalize referral agreements with regional sleep clinics to funnel eligible participants into Bonn's residential unit while aligning screening criteria and consent processes.
Launch targeted outreach to neighboring university hospitals and neurology clinics to broaden referrals and reduce pre-screening backlogs.
Deploy mobile pre-screening clinics at community centers to identify eligible participants efficiently while maintaining ethical consent and eligibility verification.
levers.review_lever: Regional recruitment reduces enrollment time but increases multi-site coordination overhead; the three options leave unaddressed how to ensure uniform data quality controls and IRB alignment across partners.

levers.name: Tiered sensing calibration and data quality management
levers.consequences: A more aggressive sensing approach improves data resolution and reduces manual review burden, but it raises equipment costs, training needs, and daily maintenance demands. This trade-off constrains staffing flexibility and requires ongoing vendor support.
options: Fully implement nightly dry-electrode EEG headbands with automated artifact rejection to standardize data capture and reduce technician workload.
Maintain the current tiered approach but add randomized mid-study nights with enhanced PSG to validate data fidelity and artifact handling.
Limit enhanced nights to participants with flagged events to conserve resources while risking missed captures of infrequent episodes.
levers.review_lever: Automated artifact rejection reduces manual scoring but relies on robust calibration; gaps include potential misclassification during artifact-rich periods and the need for ongoing validation.

levers.name: Governance of data sharing and privacy versus collaboration
levers.consequences: Expands collaborative opportunities by improving data accessibility while maintaining privacy safeguards; however, broader sharing increases compliance workload and potential delays in data release.
options: Finalize de-identification standards and access controls to enable broader secondary analyses while preserving video data privacy.
Negotiate tiered data-use agreements with external researchers to balance openness with institutional IP protections and governance frameworks.
Implement a controlled-access data portal with audit trails and reviewer workflows to vet research requests before data release.
levers.review_lever: Broad data sharing raises privacy management overhead and potential slowdowns; the three options do not specify how to enforce timely reviews or monitor breaches.

levers.name: Safety-first staffing and operations protocol
levers.consequences: Strengthened coverage and rapid response during nights improve participant safety and data integrity, but may increase training costs and complicate scheduling. This requires ongoing supervision to maintain morale and competency as the program scales.
options: Institute an on-call, cross-trained technician pool to cover peak nights and maintain safety without expanding full-time headcount.
Adopt a staggered shift schedule with backup rosters to ensure continuous coverage during high-risk periods.
Deploy automated alarm escalation systems paired with periodic drills to reduce response times while maintaining minimal on-site presence.
levers.review_lever: On-call staffing enhances safety but can incur idle-time costs and scheduling complexity; gaps include how to sustain morale and training efficiency as capacity scales.

levers.name: Funding structure and publication rights strategy
levers.consequences: This lever clarifies incentives and risk sharing; diversification reduces dependency on any single partner but may slow procurement cycles and complicate governance.
options: Negotiate industry partnership terms that preserve publication rights while offering milestone-based funding and explicit pre-publication review windows.
Pursue diversified funding from foundations and government grants to reduce reliance on industry partnerships and streamline administration.
Establish staged IP and data-access agreements that allow external researchers to reproduce methods while safeguarding core datasets.
levers.review_lever: Partnership terms influence publication timelines and IP control; gaps include ensuring consistent enforcement across partners and preventing data access bottlenecks.

levers.name: Analytics validation and cross-cohort benchmarking
levers.consequences: Formal validation elevates methodological credibility and reproducibility, enabling robust phenotyping; however, it may slow iterations and require external data access commitments.
options: Establish a formal validation plan with predefined event-triage metrics and independent scoring audits to ensure reproducibility.
Implement a rolling six-month performance review with recalibration triggers when sensitivity or specificity drift is detected.
Pilot cross-site replication using matched external datasets to assess generalizability of parasomnia phenotyping across other populations.
levers.review_lever: Validation rigor strengthens credibility but adds latency; gaps include how to resolve discrepancies between internal scorers and external benchmarks when conflicts arise.

responses.strategic_rationale: Plan emphasizes a disciplined path to scale a residential parasomnia unit while preserving data quality, safety, and publication integrity. Core tensions include when to expand capacity, how to validate semi-automated event-triage without sacrificing scoring rigor, how to govern privacy without stifling collaboration, how to diversify recruitment without compromising comparability, how to pace equipment upgrades with learning milestones, and how to optimize staffing without inflating costs. levers.name: Conditional expansion of suites based on pilot data quality and safety metrics
levers.consequences: Expanding capacity beyond eight suites will enable larger cohorts and more robust longitudinal data, but only if pilot data quality, annotation throughput, and safety metrics are consistently met. A failure to meet these thresholds risks underutilization of new suites and a spike in post-event review workload that strains staffing. The downstream effect could delay Aim 2 analyses and erode early data quality momentum.
options: Expand to 12 suites only after the pilot demonstrates consistent data quality across nights, acceptable false-alarm rates, and robust annotation throughput in two consecutive cohorts.

Maintain eight suites while aggressively improving scoring throughput and enrollment efficiency to buy time before expansion.
levers.review_lever: Gating expansion concentrates risk on pilot outcomes; the three options leave unaddressed the possibility that pilot cohorts do not generalize across a larger facility, especially if late-batch nights introduce new noise.

levers.name: Adaptive event-triage enhancement through staged validation
levers.consequences: A staged validation approach for event-triage will gradually improve accuracy and reduce manual load, but initial deployment may delay full automation gains and keep part of the review work manual longer. options: Pilot a machine-assisted scoring workflow that flags high-likelihood parasomnia events for rapid dual scoring by the team.
Implement iterative error-analysis sprints to methodically reduce false positives and improve true-positive capture before full deployment.
Adopt a tiered review schedule where borderline events receive expedited expert adjudication within 24 hours of detection.
levers.review_lever: The trade-off is between speed and accuracy: faster automation may come at the cost of initial misclassifications, and the three options leave gaps in how to handle persistent edge cases.

Pilot a regional data-sharing consortium with partner sites under joint governance to exchange only structured physiological data.
levers.review_lever: The primary trade-off is speed versus privacy; three options defer broader sharing, but do not fully resolve how to balance rapid dissemination with privacy guarantees.

levers.review_lever: The trade-off is breadth versus consistency; while wider channels may improve numbers, they may challenge uniform pre-screening and baseline comparability across cohorts.

levers.review_lever: The main trade-off is cost containment versus speed to richer data; the options leave unaddressed the risk of future supply chain delays affecting critical milestones.

system_prompt:
You are an expert strategic analyst. Generate solution space parameters following these directives:

1. **Output Requirements**
   - You must generate 5 to 7 levers per response.
   - Each lever's `options` field must contain exactly 3 qualitative strategic choices as plain strings.

2. **Lever Quality Standards**
   - Consequences: describe the direct effect of pulling this lever, then at least one downstream implication or trade-off. Be concise and grounded — only cite specific numbers if the project context provides evidence for them. Do not fabricate percentages or cost estimates. Target length: 2–4 sentences.
   - Options MUST:
     • Represent genuinely distinct strategic pathways (not just labels)
     • Include at least one unconventional or non-obvious approach
     • NO prefixes (e.g., "Option A:", "Choice 1:")

3. **Strategic Framing**
   - Name each lever using language drawn directly from the project's own domain — avoid formulaic patterns or repeated prefixes
   - Frame options as complete strategic approaches
   - Ensure levers challenge core project assumptions

4. **Validation Protocols**
   - For `review_lever`:
     A short critical review — identify the primary trade-off this lever introduces, then state the specific gap the three options leave unaddressed.
     Examples:
     - "Switching from seasonal contract labor to year-round employees stabilizes harvest quality, but the idle-wage burden during the 5-month off-season adds a fixed cost that erases the per-unit savings unless utilization reaches year-round levels."
     - "Each additional clinical site requires its own IRB approval, site-initiation visit, and staff credentialing — a sequential overhead that compounds rather than parallelizes, so doubling site count does not halve enrollment time."
     - "Pooling catastrophe risk across three coastal regions reduces expected annual loss on paper, but a single regional hurricane season can correlate all three simultaneously, turning the diversification assumption into a concentration risk at the worst possible moment."
     Do not use square brackets or placeholder text.

5. **Prohibitions**
   - NO prefixes/labels in options (e.g., "Option A:", "Choice 1:")
   - NO generic option labels (e.g., "Optimize X", "Tolerate Y")
   - NO placeholder consequences or bracket-wrapped templates
   - NO fabricated statistics or percentages without evidence from the project context
   - NO marketing language (e.g., "game-changing", "cutting-edge", "revolutionary")

6. **Length Limits**
   - Keep each `review_lever` to one sentence (20–40 words). State the trade-off and the gap concisely.
   - Each option should be a concrete, actionable approach (at least 15 words with an action verb) — not a short label or vague aspiration
   - Maintain parallel grammatical structure across options
   - Ensure options are self-contained descriptions

File 'plan.txt':
Plan:
Establish a 3-year residential longitudinal research unit in Bonn, Germany, for the study of adult NREM parasomnias — sleepwalking, confusional arousals, and sleep terrors — with a secondary exploratory arm for REM sleep behavior disorder under a separate protocol with dedicated neurologic screening, reflecting RBD's distinct clinical trajectory per current AASM guidance. The facility is affiliated with University Hospital Bonn's Department of Epileptology, leveraging its existing long-term video-EEG monitoring culture, and addresses a specific methodological gap: traditional single-night polysomnography rarely captures infrequent parasomnia events, while outpatient actigraphy lacks physiological resolution. The unit houses 8 active sleep suites at launch in a converted residential property in a quiet Bonn neighborhood, renovated for safety (padded corridor edges, restricted-opening windows, silent exterior door alarms, fire safety, acoustic treatment, network cabling, accessibility modifications) while preserving a domestic feel — if the environment is too clinical, naturalistic behavior is suppressed. Physical capacity exists for 12 suites, but expansion is deferred until the pilot proves acceptable data quality, manageable false alarm rates, safe staffing ratios, and usable annotation throughput. Sensing uses a tiered acquisition model: nightly low-burden monitoring via dry-electrode EEG headbands, contact-free mattress sensors, unobtrusively mounted infrared cameras, ambient microphones, and environmental sensors; scheduled enhanced nights with fuller PSG montage including standard scalp EEG, EOG, chin EMG, and leg EMG on the first night, one mid-stay night, and the final night per participant; and escalation nights deploying full PSG after technician-flagged events to capture recurrence at clinical-grade resolution. All streams are time-synchronized and stored in EEG-BIDS-compatible format on a local NAS with nightly encrypted backup to university storage, annotated in real time by the night technician and later scored by two independent raters using AASM criteria with inter-rater reliability reported. Public data sharing is limited to de-identified physiological and sensor data under data use agreements — bedroom video carries severe privacy constraints and is not deposited in public repositories. The scientific program has three explicit aims: Aim 1, establish and operationally validate the residential capture model as safe, ethics-approved, and sustainable; Aim 2, characterize within-person and between-person parasomnia patterns longitudinally, including episode frequency, morphology, triggers, and temporal clustering; Aim 3, develop and benchmark semi-automated event-triage tools that rank probable parasomnia episodes and reduce manual review burden, evaluated against dual human scorer agreement rather than promising autonomous diagnosis.

Participant recruitment targets adults aged 18–65 with NREM parasomnia confirmed through a structured pre-admission pathway: specialist clinical interview, collateral history from bed partner or household member where available, prior or screening polysomnography, and a structured exclusion checklist adjudicated by the PI. Explicit exclusions are nocturnal epilepsy or suspected epilepsy mimics, untreated obstructive sleep apnea, active major substance use disorder, severe psychiatric instability, and wandering or injury risk beyond facility capability. Recruitment channels are the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic, regional neurologist referrals, and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin network, with per-night compensation of €80 plus meals. A matched control group provides baseline nocturnal movement, arousal patterns, and false-positive sensor activity under identical residential monitoring conditions, enabling benchmarking of the event-triage tools against normal nocturnal behavior. Event-yield planning assumes that based on the inclusion criterion of at least 2 self-reported episodes per month, approximately 70–80% of admitted participants will produce at least one captured and adjudicated event during a 2–8 week stay; stays may be extended up to 2 additional weeks for participants with zero captured events after the initial period, capped at 10 weeks total, with a protocol ceiling of 20% unproductive admissions before triggering a recruitment-criteria review. The core team is 9 people: a PI who is a board-certified sleep medicine physician, 2 postdoctoral researchers in sleep neurophysiology and computational neuroscience respectively, 3 research technicians rotating night shifts to ensure safe coverage of 8 active suites with adequate margin for event response and annotation, a clinical psychologist specializing in sleep disorders, a data engineer managing the sensor pipeline, and a study coordinator handling recruitment, consent, scheduling, and ethics compliance.

Budget is €3.8 million over 3 years, gated: €1.8M year one covering property lease and renovation at approximately €750K, equipment at approximately €450K, staff hiring accounting for German social insurance contributions and actual overnight coverage, ethics approval, and a pilot cohort of 15–20 participants; €1.2M year two covering full operations with 30–35 participants, the enhanced-night PSG program, first publications, and event-triage algorithm development; €800K year three conditional on demonstrable progress by month 24. Personnel costs are approximately €2M over three years and remaining funds cover participant compensation, independent scoring time, data storage and retention, regulatory and legal work, and contingency. Funding sources are DFG research grant and University of Bonn internal research funding as the primary pillars, with a pharmaceutical industry partnership as optional upside rather than a feasibility requirement — if secured, the academic team retains full publication rights with the pharma partner receiving a 30-day pre-publication comment window only. Success criteria at 36 months: safe residential monitoring operations sustained for at least 24 months, enrollment of 50–70 NREM parasomnia participants plus matched controls, capture of a prespecified minimum number of independently adjudicated parasomnia events sufficient for Aim 2 phenotyping analysis, 2–3 peer-reviewed publications in sleep medicine journals covering methods validation and longitudinal characterization, a benchmarked semi-automated event-triage model with reported sensitivity, specificity, and agreement against dual human scoring, de-identified physiological dataset deposited in a recognized repository, and a submitted phase-two grant proposal for expansion and intervention studies. Failure triggers: if by month 18 the facility has enrolled fewer than 25 participants or captured fewer than 40 adjudicated events, the program undergoes external review. Governance is a 3-member external scientific advisory board reviewing progress every 6 months, with the PI holding operational authority and budget reallocations above €50K requiring board approval. Banned words: AI, blockchain, app, VR, AR, gamification, wearable startup, consumer product, DAO, NFT, metaverse, smart home, autonomous diagnosis, digital therapeutic, SaaS, marketplace, validated (in the context of claiming a mature deployable system). Pick a realistic scenario — this is an early-stage clinical research facility producing methods validation and phenotyping work, not a finished diagnostic platform.
